# ADR-0007: articles.db owns article text; markdown files are a derived live export

## Status

Accepted (2026-07-10, not yet implemented).

## Decision

Article text had two unsynchronized owners: the markdown files and `articles.db`. The database is now the single source of truth; it serves every query and will carry revisions, alias links, and repair state. Markdown files keep being written on every ingest and revision, but as a declared derived export: regenerable from the store and checked against it by content hash in a doctor command, so divergence becomes a detectable defect instead of an ambiguity.

- Files own, DB derived: rejected, revisions/alias links/repair state do not fit frontmatter, and every query already crosses the DB.
- On-demand export only: rejected, it kills established file-reading workflows for no architectural gain.

# ADR-0004: One opaque article ref; deterministic chunk refs

## Status

Accepted (2026-07-10, not yet implemented).

## Decision

An article has exactly one public identity: `art-<yyyymmdd>-<hex8>` (acquisition date plus 8 random hex characters, the repo's run-id style), minted once by Feed at first acquisition and carrying no publisher, title, or URL semantics. Chunk refs derive from it deterministically: `<article_ref>#r<revision>:<start>-<end>` for span chunks (half-open character offsets in UTF-16 code units into that revision's stored body) and `<article_ref>#p:<post_id>` for live-update chunks. Identity lives in the ref; everything informative (title, publisher, URL, dates, hashes) lives in response fields. Only Feed mints refs: consumers deriving their own identities for feed content (as the pipeline adapter did with a projection hash) is banned. `url_hash`, `content_hash`, and `title_hash` remain internal dedup attributes and never cross the boundary.

## Considered options

- Promote the legible file ids (`art-<date>-<site>-<slug>`) to public refs: rejected. Embedded site/date/title invite parsing (Hyrum's law) and become lies after alias flips (ADR-0006) or upstream corrections; the current minting also has a live collision defect (the filename gets a dedup counter, the id does not; 13 shared-id pairs exist across the 21,138 article rows as of 2026-07-10).
- Typed-prefix ULIDs: rejected. Monotonicity at scale is a property we do not need, and it breaks the repo's legible date+hex token style.

## Consequences

- Deterministic chunk-ref derivation is what lets the chunk layer stay a rebuildable index (ADR-0008) without breaking refs anyone holds.
- The span unit (UTF-16 code units) is part of the public contract and needs a non-ASCII fixture test.
- Backfill mints refs for every existing article; old file ids remain as file names only.

# ADR-0005: Articles revise in place; re-fetch only through the repair queue

## Status

Accepted (2026-07-10, not yet implemented).

## Decision

Re-acquiring the same URL with materially changed content updates the same article as `revision + 1`; it never creates a new article. Old revision bodies are retained and stay dereferenceable (labeled superseded); search indexes only the latest revision. Automatic re-fetching happens only for quality-flagged acquisitions (suspected truncation or extraction damage) through a repair queue drained by the next Scan, plus a manual refresh command. What forced this: acquisition was one-shot (`fetched_urls` gates a URL forever), so truncated extractions could never heal, and nothing schema-level prevents same-URL duplicate rows once re-fetching exists.

## Considered options

- Automatic second-look re-fetch of every article after 24-48h: rejected, roughly doubles browser-quota spend on mostly unchanged pages.
- Manual refresh only: rejected, in practice truncations would never get repaired.

## Consequences

- Revision comparison uses normalized bodies, so whitespace-level scrape noise cannot mint revisions.
- One row per URL becomes schema-enforced.
- Live-blog articles are exempt: their mutability is per Live update, not per revision.
